sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Satyagraha**: The core mechanism involving 'Truth-force' and 'Non-violence' (Ahimsa) as a weapon of the strong, not the weak.
• **Mass Mobilization**: The shift from elite-led petitioning to the inclusion of peasants, workers, and students in the political process.
• **Non-Cooperation**: The strategic withdrawal of support from colonial institutions (courts, schools, legislatures) to paralyze the administration.
• **Key Metric**: The transition from 'Constitutional Agitation' (Moderate era) to 'Extra-Constitutional Mass Action' (Gandhian era).

items.definition: Gandhiji's strategy to build internal strength through Khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, and removal of untouchability to prepare the masses for struggle.
The internal debate within INC (1922-23) on whether to enter legislative councils (Swarajists) or continue mass struggle/constructive work (No-Changers).

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Champaran/Kheda/Ahmedabad**: The 'Laboratory' experiments for testing mass struggle techniques.
• **Nagpur Session (1920)**: The formal adoption of the goal of 'Swaraj' through peaceful and legitimate means.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Maintaining non-violence during mass fervor (e.g., Chauri Chaura incident).
• **Solutions**: Periodic suspension of movements to prevent state-led repression and ensure ideological discipline.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'K-R-J-N' (Khilafat, Rowlatt, Jallianwala, Nagpur).
• **Decoded Meaning**: The sequence of triggers leading to the 1920 Non-Cooperation movement.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 'Nagpur Session' (1920) with the 'Calcutta Session' (1920). Nagpur is where the Non-Cooperation movement was formally ratified.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Mass-based politics' vs 'Elite-based politics' to contrast the Gandhian era with the Moderate era.

keyTakeaways: Mass struggle was not just a protest but a tool for political socialization of the Indian masses.
The decision to launch a struggle was always preceded by a 'Constructive Programme' to ensure sustainability.
The internal tension between 'Council Entry' and 'Mass Struggle' defined the INC's political evolution in the 1920s.
